templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Instead of), passage-final blank
items.passage: Weaver ants construct their nests in the forest canopy by pulling living leaves together, sometimes linking their bodies into chains to bridge the gaps. Instead of producing silk themselves, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: larvae held in the jaws of adult workers supply the silk that binds the leaves together.
the leaves are bound together by adult workers with silk from larvae held in their jaws.
adult workers bind the leaves together with silk from larvae held in their jaws.
the binding of the leaves by adult workers depends on silk from larvae held in their jaws.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes ants that do not produce silk themselves, and the sentence goes on to say that the silk comes from larvae, so the phrase must describe the adult workers. Choice C places “adult workers” right after the phrase, making clear that the adult workers, not the larvae or the leaves, are the ones that do not make silk.

A.why_wrong: “Larvae” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the larvae do not produce silk themselves, even though they supply it.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
B.why_wrong: “The leaves” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the leaves, rather than the ants, avoid producing silk.

D.why_wrong: “The binding of the leaves” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that an act of binding does not produce silk itself.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (weaver ants, Oecophylla, which bind leaf nests with silk from larvae held by workers). Strong band 6 to the brief (template has a band-7 official, but the cell asks for 6). Recipes W, V, N (b1 to b3 used W/P/E, P/E/W, W/E/N). Opener word "Instead of" not used in b1 to b3. "Themselves" in the opener needs a plural noun that does not make silk; only the adult workers fit. Every option read in the full sentence: only C attaches the opener to the workers. Key is the shortest option. Blind solve: C.

band7.why: band_target 6 by the plan. The right subject is the plain agent (“adult workers”), as in 3.15 and 3.18, not a property or “that of” subject, and each wrong option fails on its subject noun alone; a sound strong band 6.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Cultivated with), passage-final blank
items.passage: Because most soil bacteria cannot be cultivated under laboratory conditions, the antibiotics they might produce have largely gone unexamined. In 2015, researchers described a device that allows such microorganisms to proliferate within their native soil. Cultivated with this device from a sample collected in a grassy field in Maine, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Eleftheria terrae produces teixobactin, an antibiotic that kills several kinds of disease-causing bacteria.
the researchers found that Eleftheria terrae produces teixobactin, an antibiotic that kills several kinds of disease-causing bacteria.
the production of teixobactin, an antibiotic that kills several kinds of disease-causing bacteria, was traced to Eleftheria terrae.
Eleftheria terrae’s antibiotic, teixobactin, kills several kinds of disease-causing bacteria.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that was cultivated with the device from a soil sample, which can only be a microorganism. Choice A places the bacterium’s name, “Eleftheria terrae,” right after the phrase, making clear that the bacterium, not the researchers or the antibiotic, was cultivated from the sample.

B.why_wrong: “The researchers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the researchers were cultivated with the device from a soil sample.

C.why_wrong: “The production of teixobactin” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that an act of production was cultivated from a soil sample.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “antibiotic,” not the bacterium, so the sentence illogically says that the antibiotic itself was cultivated with the device from a soil sample.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (teixobactin, an antibiotic made by the soil bacterium Eleftheria terrae, which was cultivated in its native soil with a diffusion-chamber device from a sample taken in a field in Maine, reported 2015; known well; no researcher named). Replaced in review: Ideonella sakaiensis, the 2016 plastic-eating bacterium, is a widely reported headline. Strong band 6. Recipes W, N, P. The antibiotic is never offered as a plain subject. Blind solve: A.

band7.why: band_target 6 by the plan. The key's subject is the organism the opener plainly describes (3.1's shape), not a property, possessive or “findings from” subject as in 2dd1b8bf, fced396a and 8b017d4e, so it sits at band 6.

fixes: subject replaced: Ideonella sakaiensis (the 2016 “plastic-eating bacterium”) is a widely reported headline subject; new subject teixobactin and Eleftheria terrae (claimed in claims.txt), same template, key letter A and recipes W, N, P
every option re-read in the full sentence: only A attaches “Cultivated with this device ...” to the bacterium
“have gone unexamined” softened to “have largely gone unexamined” after the second blind

second_blind.note: independent solve (separate agent) from passage, stem and options only; second option: none real; weak case for D (opener on “Eleftheria terrae’s antibiotic”) fails because the head is “antibiotic”, which is not cultivated

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener describing a part of the plant, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Puya raimondii, a colossal Andean relative of the pineapple, may persist for decades as a rosette of rigid, spiny leaves. A stalk that rises several meters above that foliage and bears thousands of individual flowers, ______ only once, after which the entire plant withers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Puya raimondii produces its flower spike
there is a flower spike that Puya raimondii produces
the growth of Puya raimondii’s flower spike occurs
the flower spike of Puya raimondii appears
items.explanation: The opening noun phrase describes a stalk that rises above the plant’s foliage and bears flowers, which is the flower spike, not the whole plant. Choice D places “the flower spike of Puya raimondii” right after the phrase, making clear that the spike is the stalk being described.

A.why_wrong: “Puya raimondii” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the whole plant is a stalk rising above its own foliage.

B.why_wrong: “There” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun to describe; the flower spike appears only later, inside the clause.

C.why_wrong: “The growth” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that a process of growth is a stalk that bears flowers.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Puya raimondii, Andean bromeliad that flowers once after decades and then dies). Template has no band-7 official items, so written as a strong band 6 and band_target set to 6 (plan asked for 7). Move: the opener describes a part (the stalk above the leaves), so the obvious noun, the plant, is the trap (A); the stalk is said to rise above "that foliage", so the plant itself cannot be the stalk. Recipes W, E, N (all four options name Puya raimondii, so only the head noun differs). Option lengths 40 to 52 characters; key not the longest. Blind solve: D.

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7. Strong band 6: the opener describes a part (the stalk above “that foliage”), so the obvious noun, the plant itself (A), is the trap.

items.subtype: Possessive determiner before its antecedent (14 words later), singular nouns on both sides of the blank
items.passage: Elephant seals spend months at sea, where resting at the surface would expose them to predators, particularly sharks. A study that monitored seals’ brain activity determined that once REM sleep relaxes ______ muscles, typically after an interval of slow-wave sleep spent gliding passively downward, the sleeping animals turn upside down and descend in a corkscrew-like spiral.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The muscles belong to the seals, which this sentence calls “the sleeping animals” only after the blank. The plural possessive determiner “their” agrees in number with the plural noun “animals.”

A.recipe: wrong number possessive, matching the nearest singular noun
A.why_wrong: The singular “its” does not agree with the plural “animals”; none of the singular nouns near the blank (“activity,” “REM sleep,” “interval”) can have muscles.

C.why_wrong: “It’s” is the contraction of “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.

D.why_wrong: “They’re” is the contraction of “they are,” not a possessive determiner.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (northern elephant seals sleep at sea during deep dives: slow-wave sleep while gliding, then REM sleep with the muscles slack and a corkscrew descent; Kendall-Bar et al., Science, 2023; known well; no researcher named). Hardened in review: the determiner now comes 14 words before its antecedent (“the sleeping animals”), with only singular nouns in a six-word window on either side (“REM sleep”, “interval”) and 23 run words after the blank. No singular noun in the passage can own muscles (no singular seal, animal or body), so “its” is not defensible. Blind solve: their.
band7_moves: antecedent ("the animals") about 15 words before the pronoun, as in 18382e67
singular nouns ("spiral", "REM sleep") sit between antecedent and blank, so the wrong-number determiner matches the nearest noun

band7.why: As written it read band 6: the blank ended the passage 15 words after “the animals”, “seals’” and “colleagues” also pointed to “their”, and the only singular nouns between (“spiral”, “REM sleep”) could not own muscles, so one look back settled it. Rewritten so the determiner comes before its antecedent, as in 0bcb4417: “the sleeping animals” arrives 14 words after the blank, only singular nouns sit within six words either side, and 23 run words follow the blank. No singular noun in the passage can own muscles, so the hardening adds no second answer.

fixes: band 6 as written (blank at the end, plural cues “seals’”, “colleagues”, “animals” before it, and no singular noun that could own muscles); hardened by putting the determiner 14 words before its antecedent (“once REM sleep relaxes ______ muscles, typically after an interval of slow-wave sleep spent gliding passively downward, the sleeping animals ...”), the 0bcb4417 move in a different frame from b2's “During ______”; named researcher dropped (“A study that monitored ...”)
singular-noun scan: sea, surface, study, brain activity, REM sleep, interval, slow-wave sleep, spiral; none can own muscles, so only “their” works; it’s and they’re are contractions
explanation, A why_wrong, notes and subtype rewritten
“following an interval ...” read as an unclear attachment in the second blind; now “typically after an interval ...”, an adverbial of time inside the once-clause

second_blind.note: independent solve (separate agent) from passage, stem and options only; second option: none real; “its” could point only to “A study” or “REM sleep”, neither of which has muscles

items.subtype: Finite main verb after a subject carrying two relative clauses
items.passage: Paper tubes, which Japanese architect Shigeru Ban first experimented with in the 1980s and which volunteers can easily carry and assemble without heavy equipment, ______ Ban with a dependable material for emergency shelters after earthquakes in Japan, Turkey, and India.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Paper tubes” is followed by two relative clauses (“which . . . 1980s” and “which . . . equipment”), and the sentence still needs a main verb. The finite verb “have provided” supplies it and agrees with the plural subject.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: The participle “providing” leaves the sentence with no main verb; the verbs “experimented” and “carry and assemble” belong to the relative clauses.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having provided” is nonfinite, so the sentence has no main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
D.why_wrong: The infinitive “to provide” is nonfinite, so the sentence has no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: arts (architecture; Shigeru Ban's paper-tube Paper Log House shelters after the 1995 Kobe, 1999 Turkey and 2001 Gujarat earthquakes; known well). Template has no band-7 official items, so written as a strong band 6 and band_target set to 6 (plan asked for 7). Hard settings: 22 words between the subject head and the blank, two relative clauses with their own finite verbs, 15 words after the blank; not the dash-list frame of 3.13. With each distractor the sentence has no finite main verb. Blind solve: have provided.

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7. Strong band 6: 22 words and two relative clauses with their own finite verbs stand between the subject and the blank, with 15 words after it.

items.subtype: Compound subject, each conjunct carrying a relative clause with a singular verb; plural key
items.passage: Approximately every 48 years, a bamboo species that dominates the forests of Mizoram, India, flowers synchronously and then dies. The enormous quantity of fruit that the bamboo releases and the explosion in the rodent population that this temporary abundance of food generates ______ famine to the region, since the rats then turn to farmers’ crops once the fruit runs out.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is compound: “the enormous quantity of fruit . . . and the explosion in the rodent population,” joined by “and.” The plural verb “bring” agrees with this plural subject.

A.recipe: wrong number, agreeing with the nearest noun
A.why_wrong: The singular “brings” agrees with “food” or “explosion” alone, not with the compound subject “quantity . . . and . . . explosion.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “has brought” does not agree with the plural compound subject.

D.why_wrong: The singular “is bringing” does not agree with the plural compound subject.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (mautam, the roughly 48-year mass flowering of Melocanna bamboo in Mizoram, India, followed by rat outbreaks and famine; known well; species named only as "a species of bamboo"). Band-7 settings: compound subject whose two conjuncts each hold a relative clause with its own singular verb ("releases", "generates"), only singular nouns between the first head and the blank, singular verb "generates" right before the blank, run of 41 words with 17 after the blank. Frame differs from c7cb5186 (no "not Z" tag) and from b1/b2 ("each ..."). Blind solve: bring.
band7_moves: compound subject whose second conjunct ends in a relative clause with its own singular verb right before the blank
plural key behind seven singular nouns
run of 41 words, 17 of them after the blank

band7.why: Meets section 5 for R1_quant_compound: a compound subject whose two conjuncts each carry a relative clause with its own singular verb (“releases”, “generates”), only singular nouns between the first head and the blank, the singular “generates” right before the blank so that “brings” sounds right, and 17 run words after the blank; the distractors are three singular forms, as in c7cb5186. The plural is forced only by the “and”, which the long first conjunct hides.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind two singular nouns (possessor phrase and appositive)
items.passage: Hawala, an informal money-transfer system based on trust, has operated in South Asia and the Middle East for centuries. Customers of a hawala broker, often a neighborhood shopkeeper, ______ money abroad without any currency crossing a border; the broker simply instructs a partner overseas to pay out the equivalent amount.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “Customers,” which is plural; “of a hawala broker” and the appositive “often a neighborhood shopkeeper” only describe it. The plural verb “send” agrees with “Customers.”

A.recipe: wrong number, agreeing with the nearest noun
A.why_wrong: The singular “sends” agrees with “broker” or “shopkeeper,” not with the plural subject “Customers.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “is sending” does not agree with the plural subject “Customers.”

C.why_wrong: The singular “has sent” does not agree with the plural subject “Customers.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics; hawala, the informal trust-based money-transfer system of South Asia and the Middle East, in which a broker has a partner abroad pay out the sum and no cash crosses the border; known well; no person named). Replaced in review: Kuuk Thaayorre's cardinal directions are the textbook linguistic-relativity example. Medium: two singular nouns (“broker”, “shopkeeper”) between the plural head and the blank. Blind solve: send.

fixes: subject replaced: Kuuk Thaayorre speakers using cardinal directions is the textbook linguistic-relativity example (Boroditsky); new subject hawala brokers (claimed in claims.txt; Jahai, Yupno, Al-Sayyid and whistled Turkish were already claimed), options sends / is sending / has sent / send, key letter D
every option re-read in the full sentence: send only

second_blind.note: independent solve (separate agent) from passage, stem and options only; second option: none; the three distractors are singular

items.subtype: Personal pronoun with verb: singular antecedent in the previous sentence, plural nouns nearer the blank
items.passage: In the 1970s, recreational divers exploring the Baltic seafloor off southern Sweden discovered the wreck of Gribshunden, a Danish royal warship that caught fire and sank in 1495. Because the Baltic’s cold, brackish waters lack the shipworms that devour submerged timber elsewhere, ______ now one of the best-preserved vessels of the late fifteenth century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the wreck of Gribshunden, the warship named in the first sentence. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with this singular antecedent.

B.recipe: wrong number pronoun, matching the nearer plurals
B.why_wrong: The plural “they” does not agree with the singular antecedent, the wreck of Gribshunden; the plural nouns just before the blank (“waters,” “shipworms”) are not what is well preserved.

C.why_wrong: The plural “those” does not agree with the singular antecedent, the wreck of Gribshunden.

D.why_wrong: “We” would mean that the writer and reader are a well-preserved ship, which makes no sense here.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology; the Danish royal warship Gribshunden, which burned and sank off southern Sweden in 1495, found by recreational divers in the 1970s and well preserved because the brackish Baltic has no shipworms; known well; no person named). Replaced in review: the 47-meter siphonophore filmed in 2020 is widely reported record trivia. Medium: plural nouns (“waters”, “shipworms”) sit between the antecedent and the pronoun, and neither can be a ship; the timbers are never named as a plural noun, so “they” has no defensible referent. No singular demonstrative or “one” beside the singular key. Blind solve: it is.

fixes: subject replaced: the 47-meter siphonophore filmed off Western Australia in 2020 is widely reported record trivia (same class as the limpet item replaced in b3); new subject the Gribshunden wreck (claimed in claims.txt; Uluburun was already used), same options and key letter A

plural lures chosen so neither can be a ship (“waters”, “shipworms”); no plural word for the wreck's timbers, which would have let “they are now one of the best-preserved ships” be argued; every option re-read: it is only

second_blind.note: independent solve (separate agent) from passage, stem and options only; second option: none real; “they are” has no plural antecedent that could be a vessel and clashes with “one of”; solver found C and D weak lures, but “those” and “we” are the official sets of 2.3, 2.4 and 2.15

items.subtype: Plural possessor + plural noun, partial grid; options carry the clause comma
items.passage: In Vietnamese water puppetry, a tradition dating back roughly a thousand years, several performers stand waist-deep in a village pond behind a bamboo screen, maneuvering lacquered wooden figures with long rods submerged beneath the surface. Because the screen and the water conceal the ______ the figures appear to glide independently.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The movements belong to the “several performers” who stand behind the screen, so the plural possessive “performers’” is needed. “Movements” is a plain plural noun and takes no apostrophe.

A.why_wrong: The singular possessive “performer’s” refers to one performer, but the text says several performers work the figures.

C.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor and needless apostrophe on the plural
C.why_wrong: “Performers” needs an apostrophe to show possession, and the plural “movements” should not have one.

D.recipe: wrong possessor number and needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: “Performer’s” is singular, and “movement’s” wrongly adds an apostrophe to a plain plural noun.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Vietnamese water puppetry, mua roi nuoc, puppeteers waist-deep behind a bamboo screen working figures with rods under the water; known well). Number cue "several performers"; no plain "performers movements" option. The singular "performer's" (A) has no referent: no single performer is named. Options carry the comma that closes the "Because" clause, as 2.14 carries its period. Blind solve: performers' movements.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular title behind an appositive full of plurals
items.passage: Brazilian writer Carolina Maria de Jesus recorded daily life in São Paulo’s Canindé favela in notebooks she salvaged from the trash. Quarto de Despejo (Child of the Dark), a selection of entries from those notebooks, ______ an immediate bestseller when it was published in 1960.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the book title Quarto de Despejo, which is singular; the appositive “a selection of entries from those notebooks” only describes it. The singular verb “was” agrees with the subject.

A.recipe: wrong number, agreeing with a nearer plural
A.why_wrong: The plural “were” agrees with “entries” or “notebooks,” not with the singular subject Quarto de Despejo.

B.why_wrong: The plural “are” does not agree with the singular subject Quarto de Despejo.

D.why_wrong: The plural “have been” does not agree with the singular subject Quarto de Despejo.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Carolina Maria de Jesus's 1960 Quarto de Despejo, diary entries from her notebooks in the Caninde favela, an immediate bestseller; known well). Medium: plurals "entries" and "notebooks" in the appositive between the singular title and the blank. Blind solve: was.

items.subtype: Simple past in an after-clause with a year, after a present-tense opening sentence
items.passage: Indian writer Ismat Chughtai’s short story “Lihaaf” (“The Quilt”) remains among the most frequently analyzed works of modern Urdu fiction. After the story ______ in a Lahore literary journal in 1942, the British colonial government charged Chughtai with obscenity, though a court later dismissed the case.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause describes an event that happened in 1942, before the government charged Chughtai, so it needs the simple past. “Appeared” matches the year and the past-tense verbs “charged” and “dismissed.”

A.recipe: present simple where the past is needed
A.why_wrong: The present “appears” does not fit an event dated 1942 and reported alongside past-tense verbs.

C.why_wrong: “Will appear” places a 1942 publication in the future.

D.why_wrong: “Is appearing” describes something happening now, not a publication in 1942.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Ismat Chughtai's "Lihaaf", published in 1942 in a Lahore literary journal, obscenity case later dismissed; known well). Medium: the present "remains" in the first sentence tempts a present form; the year sits after the blank. No present perfect offered (a dated year rules it out, but it is the form most often argued for). Blind solve: appeared.

items.subtype: Finite verb of a that-clause whose subject carries a prepositional phrase and a relative clause
items.passage: In the 1960s, Malian photographer Malick Sidibé became a fixture at the celebrations of Bamako’s young people. Critics have observed that the dancers in his black-and-white photographs, many of whom wore their most fashionable clothing for these evenings, ______ remarkably comfortable in front of his camera.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the verb of the clause that begins “that the dancers,” whose subject is separated from it by “in his black-and-white photographs” and the relative clause “many of whom . . . these evenings.” The finite plural verb “appear” completes this clause.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: “Appearing” is not a finite verb, so the clause that begins “that the dancers” would have no verb.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to appear” leaves the clause that begins “that the dancers” without a finite verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having appeared” is nonfinite, so the clause that begins “that the dancers” would have no verb.

items.notes: Subject: arts (photography; Malick Sidibé's 1960s black-and-white pictures of Bamako's young people at parties, dressed in their most fashionable clothes; known well). Reframed in review: the old frame (a compound predicate “He traveled from party to party across the city ... and ______ the dancers”, split by a dash pair around “courtyard dances ...”, with capturing / to capture / having captured / captured) copied 2.1's skeleton and option set. Now the blank is the verb of a that-clause, the architecture of 3daf126e at medium length, with a relative clause carrying its own past verb (“wore”) between subject and blank. Blind solve: appear.

fixes: frame replaced: the compound predicate “He traveled from party to party across the city ... and ______ the dancers”, split by a dash pair around “courtyard dances where teenagers twisted ...”, with capturing / to capture / having captured / captured, copied the skeleton and option set of 2.1 (“premiered her First Symphony”, dash pair, “and ______”, developing / developed / to develop / having developed); now “Critics have observed that the dancers in his black-and-white photographs, many of whom wore their most fashionable clothing for these evenings, ______ remarkably comfortable”, options appearing / to appear / having appeared / appear, key letter D
every option re-read in the full sentence: appear only

second_blind.note: independent solve (separate agent) from passage, stem and options only; second option: none; A to C leave the that-clause without a finite verb

items.subtype: Personal pronoun: subject, named woman as antecedent
items.passage: In 1901, Japanese poet Yosano Akiko published Midaregami (Tangled Hair), a collection of tanka—poems of thirty-one syllables—that openly celebrated romantic love. Over the following decades, ______ also translated the eleventh-century classic The Tale of Genji into modern Japanese, making it far easier for general readers to enjoy.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who translated The Tale of Genji is Yosano Akiko, the poet named in the previous sentence. The singular pronoun “she” refers to her.

A.why_wrong: “It” could refer only to the collection Midaregami, and a book cannot translate another book.

B.why_wrong: The plural “those” has no plural antecedent that could translate a book.

D.why_wrong: “Both” would refer to two people, but only one poet is named.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Yosano Akiko's 1901 Midaregami and her modern-Japanese translations of The Tale of Genji; known well). Easy: the antecedent is the subject of the previous sentence. No bare "they" offered (singular "they" would be defensible for a person), following 1.33's set. Blind solve: she.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head + of-phrase and singular appositive
items.passage: The eleven rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, a pilgrimage town in Ethiopia’s northern highlands, ______ carved downward into solid volcanic bedrock about eight centuries ago.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “churches,” which is plural; “of Lalibela” and “a pilgrimage town in Ethiopia’s northern highlands” only describe where they are. The plural verb “were” agrees with “churches.”

B.recipe: wrong number, agreeing with the nearest noun
B.why_wrong: The singular “was” agrees with “town,” not with the plural subject “churches.”

C.why_wrong: The singular “is” does not agree with the plural subject “churches.”

D.why_wrong: The singular “has been” does not agree with the plural subject “churches.”

items.notes: Subject: history (Lalibela's eleven rock-hewn churches, traditionally dated to around 1200; known well). Easy: one singular appositive between head and blank, as in 1.38's "of Ohio". Blind solve: were.

fixes: explanation quoted the appositive as “a town in ...”; the passage says “a pilgrimage town in ...”

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular name after a fronted participial phrase with a plural
items.passage: Constructed by thousands of laborers on a mountaintop in northern Haiti following the country’s independence from France, the Citadelle Laferrière ______ among the largest fortresses in the Americas.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “the Citadelle Laferrière,” a single fortress; the opening phrase only describes how it was built. The singular verb “is” agrees with this subject.

A.why_wrong: The plural “are” does not agree with the singular subject “the Citadelle Laferrière.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “were” does not agree with the singular subject “the Citadelle Laferrière.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “the Citadelle Laferrière.”

items.notes: Subject: history (the Citadelle Laferriere, the mountaintop fortress built in northern Haiti in the early 1800s; known well; superlative hedged to "among the largest"). Easy: subject right before the blank, frame differs from b1's name-plus-appositive. Blind solve: is.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head + appositive with a relative clause
items.passage: Penitentes, narrow blades of compacted snow that can grow taller than a person, ______ only at high elevations in arid mountain ranges such as the Andes, where intense sunlight converts snow directly into vapor through sublimation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Penitentes” is plural, as the appositive “narrow blades of compacted snow” shows. The plural verb “form” agrees with it.

A.recipe: wrong number, agreeing with a nearer singular
A.why_wrong: The singular “forms” agrees with “snow” or “person,” not with the plural subject “Penitentes.”

C.why_wrong: The singular “is forming” does not agree with the plural subject “Penitentes.”

D.why_wrong: The singular “has formed” does not agree with the plural subject “Penitentes.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (penitentes, snow and ice blades formed by sublimation in the dry high Andes; known well). Easy: the appositive ("blades") confirms the unfamiliar plural, as 1.28 does for "ayllus". Blind solve: form.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head right before the blank
items.passage: In 2017, New Zealand granted legal personhood to the Whanganui River, which Māori iwi (tribes) regard as an ancestor. Two appointed guardians ______ the river’s interests, one chosen by the iwi and one by the national government.

items.explanation: The subject “Two appointed guardians” is plural. The plural verb “represent” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The singular “represents” does not agree with the plural subject “guardians.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “is representing” does not agree with the plural subject “guardians.”

D.why_wrong: The singular “has represented” does not agree with the plural subject “guardians.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (law; Te Awa Tupua Act 2017 gave the Whanganui River legal personhood with two guardians, one named by iwi and one by the Crown; known well). Angle on the guardians rather than the headline. Easy: no intervener. Blind solve: represent.

items.subtype: Finite main verb after a subject and a short appositive
items.passage: The cable cars of Mi Teleférico, an urban transit network in Bolivia, ______ commuters between La Paz and the neighboring city of El Alto, gliding high above congested, steeply climbing streets.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “The cable cars of Mi Teleférico.” The finite verb “carry” supplies it and agrees with the plural subject “cable cars.”

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: The participle “carrying” leaves the sentence without a main verb.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to carry” leaves the sentence without a main verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having carried” leaves the sentence without a main verb.

items.subtype: Simple present: habitual cue (During the day) in a present-tense passage
items.passage: Oilbirds, nocturnal fruit-eating birds of northern South America, are among the few bird species capable of echolocation. During the day, the birds ______ in large colonies in the depths of limestone caves, where they find their way in total darkness by producing sharp clicks that are audible to humans.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes what oilbirds regularly do (“During the day”) and uses the present tense elsewhere (“are among,” “find,” “are audible”). The simple present “roost” fits this habitual action.

A.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past “roosted” clashes with the present-tense verbs around it, which describe what oilbirds do every day.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: “Had roosted” places the roosting before some other past event, but no past event is mentioned.

D.why_wrong: “Will have roosted” refers to the future, but the text describes what oilbirds do every day.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (oilbirds, Steatornis caripensis, nocturnal fruit-eating birds that roost in caves in northern South America and find their way in the dark caves with clicks audible to people; known well). Replaced in review: Lake Natron's caustic water is a viral subject (the “turns animals to stone” photographs). Easy: habitual cue in the same sentence, present verbs around it. Key letter moved from A to C so that item 20 could leave C. Blind solve: roost.

fixes: subject replaced: Lake Natron's caustic water (the viral “turns animals to stone” photographs) with its flamingos is a documentary staple; new subject oilbirds (claimed in claims.txt), options roosted / had roosted / roost / will have roosted
key letter moved from A to C to keep the batch at 6/6/6/6 after item 20 moved to A; every option re-read: roost only
blind_answer records the original option order (key A before the letter move)

second blind noted that “departing at night to forage and navigating with sharp clicks” implied echolocation while foraging (oilbirds echolocate in the caves); now “in the depths of limestone caves, where they find their way in total darkness by producing sharp clicks”

second_blind.note: independent solve (separate agent) from passage, stem and options only; second option: none real; “roosted” is grammatical alone but the present-tense, habitual context rules it out (as 1.17)

items.subtype: Singular possessor + plural noun as a verb's object, 2 x 2 grid without the plural possessive
items.passage: Alebrijes, vividly painted papier-mâché sculptures of fantastical creatures, originated in the 1930s with Pedro Linares, a Mexico City artisan who attributed the idea to a fever dream. Woodcarvers in Oaxaca later adapted the ______ to their own medium, carving similar creatures from copal wood.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The designs belong to one artisan, Pedro Linares, so the singular possessive “artisan’s” is needed. “Designs” is a plain plural (the woodcarvers adapted more than one design) and takes no apostrophe.

B.why_wrong: “Artisans” is a plain plural, so it does not show that the designs belong to Linares.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Design’s” wrongly adds an apostrophe to the plural noun “designs.”

D.why_wrong: “Artisans” lacks the apostrophe that shows possession, and “design’s” wrongly adds one to a plain plural.

items.notes: Subject: arts (alebrijes, first made by Mexico City cartonero Pedro Linares in the 1930s after a fever dream, later carved in copal wood in Oaxaca; known well). Reframed in review: “Many of the ______ combine ...” with “artisan’s figures” copied the skeleton of 1.16 (“many of the ______”, “photographer’s early photos”) and of w1b1_21 (“Many of the ______ featured”, “artist’s sculptures”); the possessor now sits in a verb's object. Cue: one named artisan. No “artisans’” option, following 1.16, so the plural woodcarvers cannot license a second answer. Key letter moved from C to A. Blind solve: artisan's designs.

items.subtype: Four spellings of one singular possessive noun, in a result clause
items.passage: Ol Doinyo Lengai, a volcano in northern Tanzania, erupts an unusual lava containing large amounts of sodium carbonate. Fluid enough to flow almost like water, this lava changes from black to white within days of solidifying, so the ______ upper slopes frequently appear to be dusted with snow.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The upper slopes belong to Ol Doinyo Lengai, a single volcano, so the singular possessive “volcano’s” is needed.

A.why_wrong: “Volcanoes” is a plain plural and does not show possession.

C.why_wrong: “Volcanoes’” is a plural possessive, but the text describes only one volcano.

D.why_wrong: “Volcano” without an apostrophe and -s does not show that the slopes belong to the volcano.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (geology; Ol Doinyo Lengai, Tanzania, erupts runny natrocarbonatite lava that turns from black to white as it weathers; known well). fixes: subject replaced: the Richat Structure (“Eye of the Sahara”, seen from orbit) is a viral subject and its “attribute the ______ circular shape” slot sat close to 1.10; new subject Ol Doinyo Lengai (claimed in claims.txt), options volcanoes / volcano’s / volcanoes’ / volcano, key letter B

items.subtype: Past perfect in a counterfactual if-clause (would have)
items.passage: Rani ki Vav, an eleventh-century stepwell in the Indian state of Gujarat, lay buried beneath silt until archaeologists excavated it in the 1980s. Its carvings are remarkably well preserved: if floods ______ the stepwell, far fewer of its sculptures would have survived.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence imagines a past that did not happen: the floods did bury the stepwell. With “would have survived” in the main clause, the if-clause needs the past perfect, “had not buried.”

A.recipe: present simple where the past perfect is needed
A.why_wrong: “Do not bury” describes the present, not the floods of centuries ago that the sentence imagines away.

B.why_wrong: “Will not bury” refers to the future and cannot pair with “would have survived.”

C.why_wrong: “Are not burying” describes something happening now, not a past event.

items.notes: Subject: history (Rani ki Vav, the 11th-century stepwell at Patan, Gujarat, silted by floods and excavated in the 1980s with its sculptures well preserved; known well). Counterfactual shape of 1.15, so it differs from the three ordered-past items in b1 to b3. Options all carry "not" so the key's negation gives nothing away. No conditional forms offered. Blind solve: had not buried.

items.subtype: Finite verb of a how-clause (compound subject)
items.passage: Ghanaian writer Ama Ata Aidoo’s first play, The Dilemma of a Ghost (1965), concerns a young Ghanaian who returns from university in the United States with an African American bride. The drama depicts how his relatives and his new wife ______ to reconcile their conflicting expectations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause beginning “how his relatives and his new wife” needs its own finite verb. The plural present-tense verb “struggle” supplies it and agrees with the compound subject.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: “Struggling” leaves the how-clause without a finite verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to struggle” leaves the how-clause without a finite verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having struggled” leaves the how-clause without a finite verb.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Ama Ata Aidoo's 1965 play The Dilemma of a Ghost: Ato returns from the United States with his African American wife, Eulalie; known well). Subordinate-clause slot (1.14 shape), unlike b3's compound predicate. Blind solve: struggle.

items.subtype: -ing participial phrase of result after a complete clause and comma
items.passage: Needle ice can develop on clear nights when the air temperature near the ground drops below freezing but the soil beneath remains slightly warmer. Moisture drawn upward by capillary action freezes at the surface in slender vertical columns, ______ pebbles and soil particles several centimeters into the air.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “Moisture drawn upward by capillary action freezes at the surface in slender vertical columns” is already complete, so the blank must begin a phrase that adds to it. The participle “lifting” begins a phrase describing what the freezing moisture does.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: “Lifts” would be a second verb joined to “freezes” by a comma alone, with no “and.”

C.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
C.why_wrong: “It lifts” creates a second independent clause joined to the first by only a comma.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (past perfect)
D.why_wrong: “Had lifted” is a finite verb with no subject or conjunction linking it to the clause, and its tense does not fit.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (needle ice: on cold nights over unfrozen soil, moisture drawn up by capillary action freezes in thin columns that lift pebbles and soil; known well).
